question: What is the crew interface to the flight management computer?

options.text: The electronic flight instrument control panel
The mode control panel
The control display unit
The display select panel

explanation: One unit is provided for each pilot, so the route can be worked on by one while the other monitors.

question: What determines whether an airplane has one or two flight management computers?

options.text: The configuration of that particular airplane
Whether the airplane is approved for RNP approaches
The number of inertial reference units installed
The maximum certificated takeoff weight

explanation: Dual installations are an option on this type. Verify the fit on your fleet against your operator FCOM.

question: What does the navigation database contain?

options.text: Only the routes flown by the operator
Terrain and obstacle data for the terrain display
Aircraft performance data only
Waypoints, navigation aids, airways, airports, runways and procedures

explanation: It is the reference from which the route is assembled, which is why a route can only be built from what the database holds.

question: For how long is a navigation database cycle valid?

options.text: 7 days
28 days
56 days
90 days

explanation: The cycle matches the international cycle for aeronautical information, so procedures change on a predictable schedule.

question: Why are two database cycles normally stored in the computer?

options.text: So that a corrupted cycle can be replaced automatically
So that two operators can use the same airplane
So the next cycle is available and can be activated when it becomes effective
So the crew can compare the two versions in flight

explanation: Loading in advance means the change of cycle does not require maintenance action on the effective date.

question: What must the crew do if a required waypoint is not in the database?

options.text: Select the nearest database waypoint instead
Request a different clearance, since it cannot be flown
Define it manually, for example by bearing and distance or by coordinates
Load it from the previous database cycle

explanation: Pilot defined waypoints extend the route beyond the database, though they carry no procedural coding with them.

question: What are the main functions of the flight management computer?

options.text: Tuning and monitoring of the communication radios
Autopilot engagement and disengagement
Position determination, lateral and vertical navigation, and performance computation
Control of the display electronic units

explanation: It is a navigation and performance computer, and the autopilot is what turns its outputs into airplane movement.

question: How does the flight management computer determine airplane position?

options.text: From the GPS receiver alone
From the air data computers and the compass system
From the inertial reference units alone
By blending inertial data with radio and satellite updating

explanation: Inertial data is smooth but drifts, while radio and satellite data is accurate but noisy, so the two are combined.

question: Why does an inertial only position degrade with time?

options.text: Because magnetic variation changes along the route
Because small sensor errors accumulate as the flight progresses
Because the units cool down during the cruise
Because the alignment is lost after a fixed period

explanation: Integration of acceleration into position means any error is integrated too, which is why external updating is needed.

question: What is entered on the position initialisation page before flight?

options.text: The departure runway and the initial climb altitude
The zero fuel weight and the cost index
The takeoff reference speeds
The airplane present position, used to start the inertial alignment

explanation: The alignment needs a starting position because the system measures change of position, not absolute position.

question: Which of the following is entered on the performance initialisation page?

options.text: The transponder code
The takeoff flap setting
The departure and arrival runways
The zero fuel weight and the cost index

explanation: Performance predictions cannot begin until the computer knows the weight it is working with.

question: What does the cost index represent?

options.text: The operator target fuel reserve
The fuel required per nautical mile
The ratio between the cost of time and the cost of fuel
The percentage of maximum range speed to be flown

explanation: It is the single number that tells the computer how to trade fuel against time when choosing a speed.

question: What is the effect of entering a high cost index?

options.text: The computed speeds decrease, favouring fuel over time
The computed speeds increase, favouring time over fuel
The cruise altitude is raised automatically
The descent is started earlier

explanation: A high index means time is expensive relative to fuel, so the computer is willing to burn more fuel to save minutes.

question: What is the effect of a cost index of zero?

options.text: Vertical navigation becomes unavailable
The speed reverts to the mode control panel selection
The computer commands maximum range speed
The computer commands maximum speed

explanation: With time valued at nothing, the only remaining objective is to minimise fuel.

question: What is defined on the takeoff reference page?

options.text: The approach and landing configuration
The cruise altitude and the step climbs
The takeoff configuration and the reference speeds
The route to the first waypoint

explanation: The speeds depend on weight, configuration and thrust, so they are computed rather than looked up.

question: What is the purpose of an assumed temperature takeoff entry?

options.text: It allows a reduced thrust takeoff by computing thrust for a higher temperature
It corrects the takeoff speeds for the actual temperature
It sets the maximum continuous thrust for the climb
It compensates the engine indications for a hot day

explanation: Telling the computer the day is hotter than it is produces a lower thrust setting that is still safe for the actual conditions.

question: Why can assumed temperature thrust reduction not be used on a contaminated runway?

options.text: Because the reduced acceleration and the degraded stopping performance cannot both be accepted
Because the engines require full thrust for anti-ice operation
Because the computer cannot calculate speeds for a contaminated surface
Because the autobrakes cannot be armed with reduced thrust

explanation: The method assumes the airplane performs as it would on a hotter day, which is not a valid assumption when braking action is degraded.

question: Where is the active route modified?

options.text: On the navigation radio page
On the legs page, with the change executed afterwards
On the performance initialisation page
On the progress page

explanation: The separation between making a change and executing it is what allows the crew to check the result before it takes effect.

question: How is a route modification displayed before it is executed?

options.text: It takes effect immediately and can be reversed afterwards
As a modification that can be reviewed or erased without affecting the active route
It is held until the next waypoint is sequenced
It is applied to the navigation display but not to the autopilot

explanation: Nothing changes until the execute key is pressed, which is why an unexecuted modification is a common source of confusion.

question: What does the progress page provide?

options.text: The list of route legs and their tracks
The departure and arrival procedures
The navigation radio tuning status
Estimated times, distances and fuel predictions along the route

explanation: It is where the plan is compared with reality, particularly the fuel remaining at the destination.

question: Why is the predicted fuel at destination monitored rather than simply noted once?

options.text: Because the computer recalculates only when the route is modified
Because winds and routing change, and the prediction changes with them
Because the reserve fuel entry changes during the flight
Because the fuel quantity indication is unreliable in the cruise

explanation: A prediction made at top of climb is worth nothing by itself, and the value of the page is in watching the trend.

question: What is the purpose of the fix page?

options.text: To fix the computed position when radio updating is lost
To hold the airplane at a selected waypoint
To define the final approach fix for a non precision approach
To create bearing and distance references from a selected fix

explanation: Drawing a range ring or a radial on the display gives a geometric reference that is independent of the route.

question: What are the three vertical phases computed by the vertical navigation function?

options.text: Acceleration, level and deceleration
Climb, cruise and descent
Departure, en route and arrival
Takeoff, cruise and approach

explanation: Each phase has its own speed and thrust logic, and the transitions between them are what the crew monitors.

question: What is the top of descent point?

options.text: The highest altitude at which the descent can be flown at idle
The point at which the descent clearance is normally issued
The point at which the cabin begins its descent
The computed position at which the descent must begin to meet the profile

explanation: It is a computed solution to a geometry and energy problem, and starting late costs either fuel or altitude compliance.

question: What is the difference between a path descent and a speed descent?

options.text: One is flown with the autopilot and the other manually
One is used above the transition level and the other below
One follows the computed vertical path while the other holds a speed
One applies to arrivals with constraints and the other to visual approaches

explanation: When the airplane cannot stay on the path at the target speed, the computer has to give up one of the two.

question: What is the effect of a headwind stronger than forecast during a descent?

options.text: The top of descent is recomputed further along the route
The airplane tends to go high on the computed path
The descent speed increases automatically
The airplane tends to go low on the computed path

explanation: Less groundspeed for the same rate of descent means the airplane covers less distance, and the geometry no longer works.

question: Why can the speedbrakes be needed during an idle path descent?

options.text: Because the idle descent is the shallowest available and cannot recover a high energy state
Because the path is computed for a clean configuration only
Because the vertical navigation function commands them automatically
Because idle thrust is not available with anti-ice in use

explanation: With thrust already at idle there is no further reduction available, so drag is the only remaining control.

question: Where are departure and arrival procedures selected?

options.text: On the departure and arrival page
On the route page
On the legs page
On the progress page

explanation: Selecting the coded procedure loads the whole sequence of legs, constraints and speeds in one action.

question: Why must a loaded procedure still be checked against the published chart?

options.text: Because the database does not contain altitude constraints
Because coding differences and database errors can exist and the crew remains responsible
Because the computer cannot fly curved legs
Because the procedure loads without its speed restrictions

explanation: Loading a procedure is a convenience, not a verification, and the chart remains the authoritative document.

question: What does the hold page allow the crew to do?

options.text: Build a holding pattern at a selected fix
Suspend the sequencing of route legs
Hold the computed position when updating fails
Hold the current altitude in vertical navigation

explanation: The entry, the inbound course and the timing are coded, and the computer then flies the pattern as part of the route.

question: What is meant by required navigation performance?

options.text: The accuracy of the inertial system after alignment
The navigation accuracy that must be achieved for the procedure being flown
The accuracy currently being achieved by the system
The minimum number of navigation aids required

explanation: It is the standard the airspace or procedure demands, and it is meaningless without the actual performance to compare it with.

question: What does an unable required navigation performance message mean?

options.text: The navigation database has expired
The system cannot guarantee the accuracy the procedure requires
The route contains a leg the computer cannot fly
The inertial units have failed to align

explanation: The airplane may still be tracking accurately, but the system can no longer assure the containment the procedure assumes.

question: Where are flight management computer messages displayed?

options.text: On the system annunciator panel
On the navigation display only
In the scratchpad of the control display unit
On the primary flight display mode annunciations

explanation: Messages appear where the crew is already working, and they remain until acknowledged.

question: What is the purpose of the flight management computer source selector?

options.text: It transfers navigation from the computer to raw data
It selects which inertial unit updates the computed position
It allows both sides to be fed from one computer if the other fails
It selects between the navigation database cycles

explanation: As with the other source selectors, the cost of the reconfiguration is the loss of independence between the two sides.

question: How can the navigation radios be tuned?

options.text: Automatically during the cruise and manually below 10000 ft
Automatically only
Manually only
Automatically by the flight management computer or manually by the crew

explanation: Autotuning supports the computed position, and manual tuning is what allows the crew to monitor a specific aid.

question: Why does the crew sometimes tune a navigation aid manually during an approach?

options.text: Because the computer cannot tune localizer frequencies
To monitor the approach with raw data independent of the computed solution
Because autotuning is inhibited below the transition level
To prevent the computer from updating its position

explanation: Raw data monitoring is the defence against a computed position that has drifted or been corrupted.

question: What does a distance measuring equipment receiver measure?

options.text: Horizontal distance over the ground to the station
Time to the station at the current groundspeed
Distance to the next waypoint on the route
Slant range from the airplane to the station

explanation: The difference between slant range and ground distance matters most when the airplane is high and close to the station.

question: When is the error between slant range and ground distance greatest?

options.text: Directly overhead the station at high altitude
During a descent through the transition level
At long range at low altitude
When two stations are used together

explanation: Overhead the station the indication approaches the height of the airplane rather than zero.

question: What does an automatic direction finder indicate?

options.text: The relative bearing to a non directional beacon
The track made good over the ground
The magnetic bearing to a VOR station
The distance to the tuned beacon

explanation: It is a bearing only aid, and it remains useful where no other navigation aid is available.

question: Why is a non directional beacon considered less reliable than a VOR?

options.text: It is affected by terrain, thunderstorms, coastlines and night effect
It has a shorter range in all conditions
It requires a receiver that cannot be autotuned
It transmits on a frequency shared with communication radios

explanation: The propagation characteristics that give it range also make it vulnerable to bending and interference.

question: What do the localizer and glideslope of an ILS provide?

options.text: Lateral and vertical guidance to the runway
Lateral guidance and distance to touchdown
Vertical guidance and a missed approach path
Distance and bearing to the runway threshold

explanation: The two beams are paired on a single frequency selection, which is why tuning one tunes both.

question: Why can the localizer signal be unreliable when an aircraft or vehicle is near the antenna?

options.text: Because the signal can be reflected and distorted, producing false deviation indications
Because the glideslope inhibits the localizer in that case
Because the receiver rejects the signal when movement is detected
Because the transmitter power is reduced automatically

explanation: Protection of the sensitive area exists for exactly this reason, and it is why low visibility procedures restrict ground movement.

question: What do marker beacons provide?

options.text: A backup localizer signal
Vertical guidance below the decision altitude
Continuous distance information along the approach
A positive indication of passing a fixed point on the approach

explanation: Each marker gives a distinct aural and visual indication, which fixes the position along the approach path.

question: What does the radio altimeter measure?

options.text: Height above the departure airport elevation
Height above the runway threshold elevation
Height above the terrain directly below the airplane
Height above mean sea level

explanation: It is a direct measurement rather than a barometric computation, which is what makes it valid for an autoland.

question: What does the weather radar detect?

options.text: Cloud
Wind shear at all ranges
Turbulence directly
Precipitation

explanation: It reflects from water droplets, which is why a dry cloud or clear air turbulence produces no return.

question: Why is a weather radar return sometimes absent from a hazardous cell?

options.text: Because the gain control suppresses distant returns
Because the radar cannot detect cells above the airplane altitude
Because ice crystals and dry hail reflect the signal poorly
Because the antenna cannot be tilted above the horizon

explanation: The top of a mature cell can appear weak on the radar while containing severe conditions.

question: What is the purpose of the radar tilt control?

options.text: It compensates for the airplane pitch attitude automatically
It selects between weather and turbulence display
It adjusts the sensitivity of the receiver
It aims the beam so that the returns come from the altitudes of interest

explanation: A fixed tilt setting looks at different heights as the range changes, so the tilt has to be worked rather than set once.

question: What does the transponder provide to air traffic control?

options.text: Identification and altitude reporting in response to interrogation
A continuous voice channel
A position report derived from the flight management computer
A datalink for route clearances

explanation: The radar picture that controllers work with depends on the airplane answering the interrogation.

question: Why is transponder altitude reporting significant beyond air traffic control?

options.text: Because it drives the cabin altitude warning
Because it provides the reference for the altitude alert
Because it updates the flight management computer altitude
Because collision avoidance systems on other aircraft depend on it

explanation: An airplane with altitude reporting inoperative cannot be given a vertical resolution by another aircraft system.

question: How many transponders are installed and how are they used?

options.text: One, with a standby unit in the equipment bay
Two, with one selected at a time
Two, both transmitting simultaneously
Three, with automatic selection of the best signal

explanation: Selecting the alternative unit is the immediate response to a suspected transponder failure.

question: What is the value of a lateral navigation route over a series of heading selections?

options.text: It allows the autopilot to be engaged at a lower altitude
It removes the need to monitor the navigation display
It guarantees compliance with altitude constraints
The airplane follows a defined track, including the turn geometry at each waypoint

explanation: Coded turns and leg transitions are what keep the airplane within the protected airspace of a procedure.

question: What is the significance of a discontinuity in the route?

options.text: The database cycle has expired for that portion of the route
The route contains a leg that exceeds the maximum leg length
The vertical profile cannot be computed beyond that point
The computer has no defined path between two points and lateral navigation will not continue through it

explanation: An unresolved discontinuity produces a surprise at exactly the moment the airplane reaches it.

question: What is the purpose of an altitude constraint in the route?

options.text: It defines the altitude at which the descent begins
It sets the cruise altitude for the flight
It requires the airplane to be at, above or below a specified altitude at a waypoint
It limits the maximum altitude for the vertical profile

explanation: The constraints are what the vertical profile is built around, and deleting one changes the whole computed descent.

question: Why must an altitude constraint be checked against the clearance actually received?

options.text: Because constraints are not loaded with the procedure
Because constraints are ignored when the autopilot is engaged
Because the coded constraint may differ from what the controller has instructed
Because the computer applies constraints only in the climb

explanation: The database reflects the published procedure, while the clearance reflects what the controller wants at that moment.

question: What happens to lateral navigation when the route is fully sequenced and no further legs exist?

options.text: The airplane continues on the last track and the crew must intervene
Lateral navigation disengages and the airplane rolls wings level
The computer reverts to the departure route
The airplane enters a holding pattern at the last waypoint

explanation: Running out of route is a configuration the crew has to anticipate, since the automation has nothing left to follow.

question: Why is satellite updating valuable to the computed position?

options.text: It replaces the need for inertial reference units
It provides accurate position independently of ground based aids
It allows the database to be updated in flight
It provides altitude for the vertical profile

explanation: It gives high accuracy anywhere, including over oceans and areas without radio navigation coverage.

question: What is the crew defence against an erroneous computed position?

options.text: Comparing the computed position with raw navigation data
Switching the navigation display to the plan mode
Reinitialising the position on the initialisation page in flight
Selecting both sides to a single computer

explanation: The computed picture looks convincing whether it is right or wrong, and only an independent source can reveal an error.

question: What does the navigation display map accuracy depend on?

options.text: The quality of the position solution behind it
The range selected on the display control panel
The number of navigation aids displayed
The database cycle in use

explanation: The map is drawn around the computed position, so a position error moves everything on the display together.
